title: Mellin evaluation turns closure into a zero-annihilator test
claim: Across the deterministic and generalized Nyman–Beurling criteria, the decisive bridge is not approximation by itself but an admissible Mellin evaluation: a putative zeta zero annihilates the transforms of the approximating span while the target transform remains nonzero. Mellin–Plancherel domination, mean-cancelling compactification, and splitting the domain at one are three concrete ways of making that evaluation continuous along the claimed closure.
historical_or_program_relation: The broad density formulation is refined first into a norm-preserving spectral factorization and later into explicit continuity templates for generalized or random kernels. This progression isolates the reusable zero-exclusion mechanism from the particular fractional-part dictionary.
limits: The continuity hypotheses are not interchangeable: the Baez-Duarte argument uses RH-dependent domination in one direction, the compact-support argument proves only zero-set inclusion unless the kernel Mellin transform is separately nonzero, and the probabilistic criterion has its own tail conditions. No one of these units proves RH or transfers every kernel between frameworks.

title: Regularization fixes local limits while leaving the Hilbert-norm bottleneck
claim: Damping the natural Möbius sums identifies the correct pointwise target and preserves each fixed coordinate, while smoothing also makes the far tail estimable; neither operation by itself supplies convergence in the Nyman–Beurling Hilbert norm. In the coordinate formulation, the unresolved mass is localized concretely to a moving intermediate window, so regularization relocates rather than removes the proof burden.
historical_or_program_relation: The strengthened Baez-Duarte criterion recasts natural approximation as a summability scheme; later coordinate analysis explains why that scheme can look locally successful yet still lack a global square-summable dominator. Proposed Cesaro or subsequence variants continue this regularization program but remain epistemically separate from the proved damped criterion.
limits: Pointwise convergence, fixed-coordinate convergence, and far-tail bounds do not imply norm convergence. The accepted record proves equivalence only for the specified damped family; the proposed Cesaro, subsequence, rate, and Lp variants are not promoted here to equivalent criteria.

title: Changing the approximation dictionary is direction-specific
claim: Restrictions or enlargements of a Nyman–Beurling dictionary preserve an RH implication only when the information they discard is audited in the relevant direction. The smaller antisymmetric difference space remains equivalent because the lost fractional-part component is quantitatively restored; the strong-kernel necessity route can drop Mellin nonvanishing, whereas the sufficiency route obtains only zero-set inclusion until nonvanishing is supplied separately.
historical_or_program_relation: These sources replace a single canonical generator family by symmetry-adapted, analytic-kernel, and probabilistic variants. Their combined lesson is a concrete design rule: necessity may tolerate a broader kernel class than sufficiency, and an apparently smaller space is safe only when its missing direction is controlled rather than silently quotiented out.
limits: The HP correction argument, the strong-kernel theorem directions, and the pNB/gNB examples use different spaces and hypotheses. They do not establish a common maximal dictionary, and the probabilistic examples explicitly show that a condition needed by one formulation need not classify another.

title: Expectation converts random dilations into deterministic Müntz kernels
claim: The probabilistic extension is connected to the deterministic strong Nyman–Beurling program by a representation identity: expectation of a fractional-part dilation becomes the negative Müntz transform of the law's survival function. Thus randomness enters through a deterministic kernel and moment-controlled norm estimates, while the earlier sum-integral/pseudo-convolution identity supplies the operator language into which that kernel can be placed.
historical_or_program_relation: The later probabilistic formulation does not merely average approximation errors; it re-encodes a probability law as a deterministic transform compatible with an established dilation-and-convolution framework. This turns distributional choices into analyzable kernel choices.
limits: The records do not state that every survival function is a strong kernel or that the 2005 closure theorems automatically apply to every random law. Moment conditions, tail regularity, and the separate pNB/gNB hypotheses remain genuine admissibility gates.

title: Farey discrepancy requires empirical centering before arithmetic symmetrization
claim: The Farey RH criteria become concrete only after two representation choices are fixed: Möbius inversion removes coprimality, and empirical-rank centering subtracts the correct deterministic triangular contribution. With that centering, Franel's quadratic discrepancy can be transformed through Bernoulli–Möbius coordinates and cyclic Dedekind symmetrization into gcd-weighted cancellation; replacing rank by interval length loses an uncontrolled residue-class fluctuation.
historical_or_program_relation: The overview's aggregate discrepancy criterion is refined by the earlier Farey analysis into the exact combinatorial and correlation mechanisms that carry it. This identifies why the L2 statistic is arithmetic rather than merely a generic equidistribution norm.
limits: The mechanism supports the Farey discrepancy side only. It supplies no bridge to the distinct cyclotomic-height criterion mentioned alongside it, and it does not turn a pointwise discrepancy estimate or naively centered statistic into an RH equivalence.

title: Small-prime extremizers make one-sided rates decisive
claim: Robin–Lagarias and Nicolas-type criteria both concentrate multiplicative behavior on integers assembled from small primes, but their proofs live or die on effective one-sided comparison. The Robin route has incompatible RH and non-RH envelopes whose separated excess eventually outruns an elementary error term; the attempted Nicolas route combines two factors converging to compensating limits without controlling whether the deficit in one is smaller than the surplus in the other.
historical_or_program_relation: Lagarias's proof shows how a prime-product extremizer can amplify prime-counting fluctuations into a bidirectional criterion and then split finite from asymptotic obligations. The later Nicolas argument exposes the missing ingredient when the same style of packaging is supported only by a two-sided limit: sign and rate must be preserved.
limits: The criteria use different arithmetic functions and normalizations, so this is a proof-burden comparison, not an algebraic identification. The gap in the later proof does not refute the cited Nicolas equivalence or RH, and the unconditional primorial limit alone supplies neither eventual sign nor an effective rate.

title: Finite verification is informative only with a certified tail mechanism
claim: Three equivalent-criterion programs separate sharply according to what controls the unobserved tail. In the Lagarias assembly, a proved asymptotic envelope reduces the remaining obligation to an exhaustive finite prefix; for the Baez-Duarte sequence, height-suppressed coefficients can delay the dominance of a hypothetical off-line zero beyond feasible computation; in the Nicolas argument, convergence to the correct limit gives no eventual one-sided inequality at all.
historical_or_program_relation: Together these cases provide a concrete hierarchy for computational evidence: finite checking can close a theorem only after an analytic tail bound, can be weak evidence when spectral defects have delayed crossover, and cannot repair a missing sign-and-rate estimate.
limits: The delay mechanism, finite-prefix closure, and surplus-versus-deficit gap are different phenomena and supply no shared numerical cutoff. The Baez-Duarte limitation relies on its explicit zero expansion and does not assert an off-line zero; the Nicolas diagnosis concerns an argument, not the truth of its criterion.

title: Logarithmic derivatives turn zero sets into sign-controlled fields
claim: Both the Eisenstein-integral and Speiser analyses use Hadamard factorization followed by logarithmic differentiation to replace a multiplicative zero set with additive contributions whose sign can be controlled. In the Eisenstein setting paired zero blocks force one-dimensional unimodality of a scalar level-set function; in the Speiser setting the functional equation and gamma asymptotics orient the logarithmic-derivative field on remote contours so the argument principle can compare zero counts.
historical_or_program_relation: The shared mechanism links two otherwise different line-zero programs: local sign control can certify the number of level-set crossings, while boundary sign control can certify a global counting relation. It shows exactly how symmetry becomes operational only after a zero-product representation is differentiated.
limits: The sign domains, auxiliary functions, and conclusions differ. Unimodality of a shifted-xi level-set function does not imply a Speiser theorem, and a contour orientation argument does not transfer the Eisenstein truncation result without its separate strip geometry and parameter inequalities.

title: Functional symmetry is an input, not a classifier of line-zero equivalences
claim: Completion and a functional equation provide a global reflection architecture, but they do not by themselves classify when an RH- or Speiser-type equivalence survives. The Eisenstein construction explicitly separates modular symmetry in the geometric variable from reflection in the spectral variable, neither of which alone yields a line-zero theorem; the Speiser comparison includes both successful extensions and computational failures for functions lacking a Riemann-type equation, so absence of that equation is not a sufficient discriminator either.
historical_or_program_relation: The L-function overview treats functional equations as one half of a two-sided architecture, while the later comparison turns that architectural role into a scope boundary: additional arithmetic or finite-structure conditions must do the classifying work, though the accepted record does not yet identify them.
limits: The negative Speiser cases are reported computational evidence rather than rigorous counterexamples, and the positive class contains extra structure not isolated here. This relation neither dismisses functional symmetry nor proposes a replacement necessary-and-sufficient condition.

title: Finite transforms encode RH through different retained invariants
claim: The Baez-Duarte and Jensen criteria both translate zeta data into finite algebraic objects, but they preserve different decisive invariants. The binomial transform of reciprocal-zeta samples is tied by an exponential generating function to the Riesz entire function and carries a critical decay exponent; Jensen polynomials use finite windows of central completed-zeta coefficients and carry real-rootedness, with theta moments and uniform saddle-point ratio expansions supplying their analyzable input.
historical_or_program_relation: These are two concrete discretizations of an analytic zero problem: one makes cancellation visible as sequence decay, while the other makes it visible as coherent polynomial hyperbolicity. Their comparison identifies the representation choice—growth exponent versus root geometry—as the source of the subsequent proof burden.
limits: No accepted unit gives a transform between the two sequences, so they are not asserted to be equivalent to each other except through RH. Checking finitely many decay values or Jensen polynomials does not establish the required asymptotic bound or universal hyperbolicity, and positive theta-moment representations alone do not prove RH.
